@jkotas  would we be open to API proposal to expose the parameterless ctor - that would tidy this up?

We want to encourage callers to pass in an extra information about the object that triggered the exception. Situations where this extra information is not available are extremely rare. I do not see a problem with callers having to pass in `null` explicitly in these rare cases.

There are no observable public API behavior changes. The ObjectName property getter [replaces `null` with empty string](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/a54a823ece1094dd05b7380614bd43566834a8f9/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/ObjectDisposedException.cs#L99) and so the ObjectName property is going to return the empty string both before and after your change.

If there were observable public API behavior changes, it is unlikely we would accept the PR.

> Also, I see there are some failing checks in the pipeline

The failures are known issues. "Build Analysis" has links to github issues that are tracking these failures.

issue_context.title: Empty string literals in Marshal.cs
issue_context.body:
While working on #34056 I noticed that for some exceptions inside `System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal` some exceptions get thrown with empty string literals. Wouldn't it be better for these empty string literals to be replaced with the string.Empty constant?

e.g.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16164903/164531111-677293e1-4060-4515-a57f-403605e2d013.png)
comments: I couldn't figure out the best area label to add to this issue. If you have write-permissions please help me learn by adding exactly one [area label](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/area-owners.md).

There is no practical functional or performance difference between `string.Empty` and `""` (`""` generates negligibly smaller IL). It is a matter of personal preference on which one to use.

For reference, the libraries subdirectory in this repo has 6_000 instances of `string.Empty` and 21_000 instances of `""`.

Issue Details
While working on #34056 I noticed that for some exceptions inside `System.Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal` some exceptions get thrown with empty string literals. Wouldn't it be better for these empty string literals to be replaced with the string.Empty constant? e.g. ![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/16164903/164531111-677293e1-4060-4515-a57f-403605e2d013.png)
Author: tudoranghelina91
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-Meta`, `untriaged`
Milestone: -
these can be replaced with `throw new ObjectDisposedException()` though.

> throw new ObjectDisposedException() though.

`ObjectDisposedException` does not have a parameter-less constructor.
It can be replaced with `new ObjectDisposedException(null)` that's tiny bit better than empty string.
Oh - I missed that it's private. Yup.

> It can be replaced with `new ObjectDisposedException(null)` that's tiny bit better than empty string.

Well, it makes more sense to me as well. I'm up to take this one too since I brought it up
Feel free to include this change in the PR you are working on.

> There is no practical functional or performance difference between `string.Empty` and `""` (`""` generates negligibly smaller IL). It is a matter of personal preference on which one to use.
> 
> For reference, the libraries subdirectory in this repo has 6_000 instances of `string.Empty` and 21_000 instances of `""`.

What am I supposed to make of this sentence in brackets, "" generates negligibly smaller IL

First use of `string.Empty` in an assembly adds about 30 bytes to the compiled binary. It is cost of encoding field reference. `""` does not have this cost. Subsequent uses of `string.Empty` have same binary size cost as `""`.

Sections in .NET binaries are padded to multiples of 512 bytes. It means that these extra 30 bytes are observable only if they push the binary into having a new 512 chunk.
Would it make sense to bulk replace to "" purely for consistency sake?

It is one of those personal style preferences issues. We are generally not trying to enforce consistency for those across the repo. I prefer `""`. [StyleCop prefers `String.Empty`](https://github.com/DotNetAnalyzers/StyleCopAnalyzers/blob/master/documentation/SA1122.md).

> First use of `string.Empty` in an assembly adds about 30 bytes to the compiled binary. It is cost of encoding field reference. `""` does not have this cost. Subsequent uses of `string.Empty` have same binary size cost as `""`.
> 
> Sections in .NET binaries are padded to multiples of 512 bytes. It means that these extra 30 bytes are observable only if they push the binary into having a new 512 chunk.

As I can see from the code below, using String.Empty twice, S2 and S3 have the same IL overhead. Am I misinterpreting this?

[demo.cs](https://sharplab.io/#v2:EYLgxg9gTgpgtADwGwBYA0AXEBLANgHwAEBmAAkICZSBhUgbwFgAoU18swgRgAZSBlTqQC8APlIAicQG5mbduR78qohdwB0AUQC2ABwwBPGSzYlV/Miq7rtew8wC+QA=)

> As I can see from the code below, using String.Empty twice, S2 and S3 have the same IL overhead. Am I misinterpreting this?

The IL text does not show you the binary size.

The experiment you can run is:

1. Compile project that has just a single type and single method that returns `""`.
2. Look at the size of `.text` sections using a tool like `dumpbin`. `dumpbin` it is part of Visual Studio C++ workload. Run `dumpbin /HEADERS <your test name>.dll` and look for:
```
...
   .text name
     934 virtual size
...
````
3. Change the method to return `string.Empty` and compile the project again
4. Look at the size of `.text` sections in the produced .dll again. You should see that it is about 30 bytes larger.

I created a new class library
```c#
using System;

namespace ClassLibrary1
{
    class C
    {
        string M()
        {
            return string.Empty;
        }
    }
}
```

```
.\dumpbin.exe /HEADERS E:\ConsoleApp3\ClassLibrary1\bin\Debug\netcoreapp3.1\ClassLibrary1.dll
```

use ""
```
SECTION HEADER #1
   .text name
     644 virtual size
```
use string.Empty
```
SECTION HEADER #1
   .text name
     660 virtual size
```

Why is there 16 bytes difference here.

> First use of `string.Empty` in an assembly adds about 30 bytes to the compiled binary. It is cost of encoding field reference. `""` does not have this cost. Subsequent uses of `string.Empty` have same binary size cost as `""`.
> 
> Sections in .NET binaries are padded to multiples of 512 bytes. It means that these extra 30 bytes are observable only if they push the binary into having a new 512 chunk.

Thank you very much for answering my question. I would like to know the same cost as "" in the follow-up. How do I understand this, and why is it 30 instead of others.

To understand the detailed reason why this difference exists, you would need to drill into the details of the binary encodings in https://www.ecma-international.org/publications-and-standards/standards/ecma-335/

The exact observed cost of the `string.Empty` reference (16 bytes you have seen vs. 30 bytes that I have quoted) varies due to number of subtle factors. For example, there are internal paddings used within the .text section, and so the exact cost of the `string.Empty` reference may vary based on the names of other types and methods in the binary.

The bottom line is that the cost is negligible, and it is not something to worry about.
